post.description:
Completes a login flow from a session the browser already holds, without asking for credentials again.

This is what makes an AuthKit custom domain worth configuring. The hosted login page lives on the organization's own hostname, so the cookie set when a consumer last signed in is a first-party cookie that comes back on the next visit. Given a fresh login `code`, this exchanges that session for the same redirect `loginConsumer` would have produced.

The session is taken from the `consumer_session` header or cookie by the request guard, which also rejects expired or revoked sessions and slides the expiry window on success.
Logs out a consumer by destroying their session

get.description: Get a consumer by their session ID

post.description: Resend a confirmation email to a consumer

get.description:
Lists the OAuth clients a consumer has connected.

A live refresh token is what makes a client "connected": it is the thing that lets the client keep issuing itself access tokens, and deleting it is what disconnecting means. Expired ones are left out — they grant nothing and the consumer cannot act on them.

delete.description:
Disconnects a client from a consumer by deleting the grant behind it.

This removes every live refresh token for the pair, so the client can no longer issue itself new access tokens. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire — they are signed JWTs that resource servers verify offline, and nothing here can reach them. Callers should say so rather than promise an immediate cutoff.

post.description: Initiates a password reset for a consumer. Always returns success to prevent email enumeration.
Resets a consumer's password using a valid reset token.

get.description:
OAuth 2.1 authorization server metadata.

The discovery document for one organization: a client fetches this to learn where to send the user, where to exchange the code, and which scopes it may ask for. Everything this document points at is itself described in this spec.

Unauthenticated — discovery has to work before a client exists.

Public keys for verifying access tokens.

A resource server fetches this to verify AuthKit's access tokens offline — the tokens are ES256-signed JWTs and are never introspected against this server. Cache the response and re-fetch on an unrecognised `kid`.

Instance-wide, not org-scoped: one signing key serves every organization, and the token's `iss` claim is what identifies the organization it was issued for.

Unauthenticated.

post.description:
Registers an OAuth client (RFC 7591).

Open registration: no initial access token, and any caller may register. This is what lets an MCP client discover the server and enrol itself without a human provisioning it first.

The client is public — it receives no secret and authenticates at the token endpoint with PKCE alone. Registration is not scoped to a consumer; it says a client exists, not that anyone has authorized it.

Errors follow RFC 7591 §3.2.2: `{"error": "<code>", "error_description": "<text>"}` with `invalid_redirect_uri` or `invalid_client_metadata`.

400.description: The request was refused. `error` says why, using the codes of RFC 6749 §5.2 or RFC 7591 §3.2.2.

get.description:
OAuth 2.1 authorization endpoint.

Send the user here in a browser to begin an authorization. The client is validated, the `redirect_uri` and requested scopes are checked, a pending authorization is stored, and the user is redirected to AuthKit's own login page. Once they sign in, AuthKit completes the flow internally and redirects back to `redirect_uri` with `code` and `state`.

There is no consent screen: signing in grants the requested scopes. Treat every registered client as first-party until that changes.

This is a browser endpoint, not an API call — the success case is a redirect, and the response is only ever consumed by a user agent following it. Errors currently render an error page rather than redirecting `error` back to the client.

post.description:
OAuth 2.1 token endpoint.

Exchanges an authorization code for an access token, or spends a refresh token for a new one. The grant is chosen by `grant_type`.

Both grants are scoped to the organization in the path: a code or refresh token issued for one organization cannot be redeemed against another, and the `iss` claim of the token returned is derived from the grant rather than from this path.

Unauthenticated in the client-credentials sense — clients are public and prove themselves with PKCE (`authorization_code`) or by holding the refresh token.

Errors follow RFC 6749 §5.2: `{"error": "<code>", "error_description": "<text>"}` with `invalid_request`, `invalid_grant` or `unsupported_grant_type`. A spent, expired or unknown refresh token is `invalid_grant` — the signal to send the user through authorization again.

400.description: The request was refused. `error` says why, using the codes of RFC 6749 §5.2 or RFC 7591 §3.2.2.

requires_confirmation.description: Whether following `redirect_url` would be refused until this consumer confirms their email. Callers should show a "check your email" prompt instead of navigating.
Whether following `redirect_url` would be refused until this consumer confirms their email. Callers should show a "check your email" prompt instead of navigating.

ResumeConsumerResponse.description: Note the absence of `loginConsumer`'s `requires_confirmation`. The only redirect that turns an unconfirmed consumer away is AuthKit's own OAuth callback, and this endpoint refuses to resume into one at all; every other redirect belongs to the organization, which is free to accept an unconfirmed consumer. So there is never a "confirm first" answer left to give.

created_at.description:
UTC, RFC 3339.

The column is a naive `timestamp`, so the instant is only conventionally UTC in the database. Asserting that here rather than passing the naive value through is what lets the schema say `format: date-time` truthfully — a value with no offset is not RFC 3339, and a client generated from a spec that claimed otherwise would fail to parse it.

GrantResponse.description: One client a consumer has connected, as the consumer would recognise it.

scopes.description: Scopes the consumer granted, split from the space-delimited stored form.

granted_at.description: When the consumer first authorized this client. UTC, RFC 3339.

last_used_at.description: When the grant was last exchanged for an access token. Clients refresh about hourly, so this trails real activity by up to the access-token lifetime. UTC, RFC 3339.

OAuthMetadata.description:
Authorization server metadata, as defined by RFC 8414.

Every endpoint named here is org-scoped except `jwks_uri`: one signing key serves the whole instance, while issuer and grants are per-organization.

issuer.description: Identifier this server uses in the `iss` claim of the tokens it signs, and the value a resource server must match against. Org-scoped: `<api_url>/<org_id>`.

authorization_endpoint.description: Where to send the user to authorize a client.

token_endpoint.description: Where to exchange an authorization code, or a refresh token, for an access token.

registration_endpoint.description: Where a client registers itself (RFC 7591). Open — no initial access token required.

jwks_uri.description: Where to fetch the public keys that verify this server's access tokens. Instance-wide, not org-scoped.

response_types_supported.description: Always `["code"]`. OAuth 2.1 removes the implicit flow.

code_challenge_methods_supported.description: Always `["S256"]`. PKCE is required, and plain challenges are rejected.

token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported.description: Always `["none"]`. Clients are public and authenticate by PKCE, not a secret.

scopes_supported.description: The scopes this organization has defined. A request for anything outside this list is rejected at the authorization endpoint.

keys.description: The keys that may have signed a live access token. Verifiers should select by `kid` rather than assuming a single entry, so that key rotation does not break them.

Jwk.description: A single public key in JWK form (RFC 7517).

x.description: Base64url-encoded x coordinate of the public point.

y.description: Base64url-encoded y coordinate of the public point.

kid.description: Key identifier. Matches the `kid` header of tokens signed with this key, and is how a verifier picks the right entry from `keys`.

client_id.description: The client's identifier. Pass this as `client_id` at the authorization endpoint. There is no client secret.

redirect_uris.description: Echoed from the request verbatim, including any entries beyond the first — which is the only one that was registered. Treat the first entry, not this array, as the registered value.

token_endpoint_auth_method.description: Always `none`. The client is public and proves itself with PKCE.

error.description: Machine-readable error code. Branch on this, not on the description.

error_description.description: Human-readable explanation, for logs and developers.

OAuthErrorCode.description: The `error` codes these two endpoints answer with.

oneOf.description: A required parameter is missing, repeated or malformed (RFC 6749 §5.2).
The code or refresh token is unknown, spent, expired, or was issued for a different `redirect_uri` or PKCE verifier (RFC 6749 §5.2).
A redirect URI in a registration is missing, not absolute, or not allowed (RFC 7591 §3.2.2).
A registration field other than `redirect_uris` is invalid (RFC 7591 §3.2.2).
Something failed on our side; retrying may help.

client_name.description: Human-readable name for the client. Shown to the consumer when they review the clients they have connected.

redirect_uris.description:
Redirect URIs the client may use. At least one is required, and every entry must be an absolute URI without a fragment: `https`, `http` on a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`), or a private-use scheme such as `myapp://callback`. Anything else is refused with `invalid_redirect_uri`.

**Only the first entry is registered.** The authorization endpoint compares `redirect_uri` against that one value and rejects anything else, so send the URI you intend to use first.

access_token.description: An ES256-signed JWT. Verify it offline against the keys at `/.well-known/jwks.json`; it is not stored server-side and there is no introspection endpoint. Carries `iss`, `sub` (the consumer), `org_id`, `scope`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat` and `jti`.

refresh_token.description: An opaque token, valid 30 days, exchangeable for a new access token at this endpoint. Rotated on every use — store this value in place of the one just spent.

TokenRequest.description:
Form body for the token endpoint. Sent as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.

Which fields are required depends on `grant_type`; the schema marks as optional every field that one of the two grants does without.

code.description: The authorization code. Required for `authorization_code`; single-use, and short-lived.

redirect_uri.description: Required for `authorization_code`. Must equal the `redirect_uri` sent to the authorization endpoint, or the exchange is refused.

client_id.description: The registered client identifier. Accepted but not currently checked against the code's own client — PKCE is what binds the exchange to the client that started it.

code_verifier.description: Required for `authorization_code`. The PKCE verifier whose S256 hash must equal the `code_challenge` sent to the authorization endpoint.

refresh_token.description: Required for `refresh_token`. Rotated on every use: the response carries a new one and the presented token stops working.

resource.description: Accepted and ignored. RFC 8707 resource indicators are not implemented.

scope.description: Accepted and ignored. The issued token carries the scope the consumer granted at the authorization endpoint; it cannot be narrowed or widened here.

consumer_session.description: Consumer session token in the `consumer_session` header
